items.title: Lost Bullet 2: Back for More
items.reason: A 98-minute French car-action sequel with an early home-invasion fight, a narcotics-unit pursuit, a substantial mid-film police-garage brawl that flows into another car chase, and extended border-road pursuits. In Review Online documents the film's opening, middle and later escalation, while The Envoy Web and The Hollywood Handle describe action recurring across the short runtime; density is therefore high but not asserted to be literally nonstop. Vehicle stunt work and pursuit dominate, with separate blunt-force melee fights and some gun violence. The car spikes, flips and collisions add spectacle, while the corrupt-police witness-protection plot adds a real but secondary conspiracy thread. Strengths include comparatively legible stunt staging, practical-looking crashes and a forceful lead. Limitations are recurrent car-chase beats, thin characterization, a conventional revenge motive, and action sequences long enough to cause fatigue. A few romantic or grief-related moments do not turn the film into relationship drama. DNA values are descriptive evidence estimates, not final eligibility or match scores.

items.title: The Transporter
items.reason: A 92-minute courier action film whose opening bank-robbery getaway leads into repeated martial-arts fights, explosions, gunfire and truck or highway stunts after a dangerous package exposes a trafficking operation. Roger Ebert's whole-film account describes action throughout; OutNow and The Washington Post confirm a strong first half but criticize a late stretch that becomes an increasingly repetitive series of fights. High action density is therefore distinct from the weaker narrative momentum and declining variety. The lead's driving skill, hand-to-hand choreography and vehicle stunts are substantial, but vehicle action is especially prominent at the start rather than evenly distributed. Riviera roads, a villa, criminal facilities and moving vehicles provide some setting changes. Weaknesses include thin human characterization, an implausible trafficking plot, formulaic romance and a noisy repetitive second half. The glossy Hong Kong-influenced practical-action visual language is evaluated as a stylistic aesthetic, not inferred from the release year. The protagonist's former military service is backstory rather than a battlefield focus. Descriptive DNA only; no final score or publication conclusion.
